reason: node-pty is used in one place, spawnTerminal in subprocess-local, for spawn, pid, onData, onExit, write, resize, pause, resume and kill. The Go harness allocates POSIX pseudo-terminals and Windows ConPTY itself on golang.org/x/sys, with no cgo and no helper executable, and keeps the master descriptor and the process handle that node-pty hides.

Upstream runs the xterm.js emulator on the host for three things: replies to terminal queries (terminal-bash), plain-text reads with wrapped rows joined and screen marks for agents, and the state behind the browser snapshot (terminal-controller). The Go harness puts a pure-Go emulator behind its own Screen interface; the module choice is provisional until a conformance test against xterm.js passes.

The addon is called once, serialize() with default options, to give a newly attached browser tab the current screen. No Go emulator read for the spec exports history, screen, cursor and modes as replayable escape sequences, so the serializer is harness code above the Screen interface, tested by replaying its output into xterm.js.

Four product packages and one test-support package use execa to run git, pnpm, gh and glab once and read the result, outside the subprocess service. Each option they rely on maps to os/exec or to a rule of the harness process package; a Run helper on that package replaces the library, and Windows batch files such as pnpm.cmd get an explicit safety rule instead of implicit handling.

No upstream source imports cross-spawn; subagent-oar declares it for the embedded third-party @botiverse/oar library, which starts vendor agent tools itself. In Go those tools are started by the harness process package, whose lookup applies PATHEXT and whose batch-file rule replaces cross-spawn's cmd.exe escaping.

No upstream source imports which; it is declared for the embedded @botiverse/oar library and is a dependency of cross-spawn. Upstream's own equivalent is resolveExecutable in subprocess-local. Go needs a short own lookup because exec.LookPath reads the harness's PATH, not the scrubbed and overridden PATH the child will receive.

forge-session uses parse to read shell commands the agent already ran and quote to build a lookup command a shell later executes. Go reads the command with the mvdan.cc/sh/v3 syntax parser, which classifies literal and dynamic words exactly, and quotes with an own single-quote function, as upstream's dependency audit recommended for this safety boundary.

125 non-test files import it: 6 in the subprocess provider, 20 product files that start programs outside the provider, 1 worker emulation, 3 test-infrastructure files and 95 build and release scripts; only spawn, spawnSync, execFile and execFileSync are used, never a shell string. Go uses os/exec inside one harness process package with operating-system owners for process trees.

The three non-test imports are release scripts that ask the operator to confirm a publish with readline.question. A Go release tool reads one line from os.Stdin with bufio and refuses when standard input is not a terminal.

ptc-runtime-node uses repl.start to evaluate model-written JavaScript while keeping variables between programs, inside a runner process. The Go host cannot evaluate JavaScript in process; under DH-ADR-4 the interpreter is a long-lived child process with piped input and output, which the process package provides. Which interpreter runs in it is left to the tool-runtime area.

Exists only because of Node: the two importing files are stand-ins in webworker-runtime that emulate Node built-ins inside a browser Web Worker (isatty always false). No upstream product code calls the real module, so there is nothing to carry into Go.

Part 1 of the patch redirects node-pty's spawn-helper path for single-file executables; Go has no helper, because the runtime sets the session and controlling terminal itself between fork and exec. Part 2 releases node-pty's Windows output worker at kill; the underlying ConPTY rule also applies to Go and is met by design: output is drained by its own goroutine and close is ordered and bounded (DH-LIB-NODEPTY-R10).

The exemption lets subprocess-local run a postinstall script that restores the executable bit on node-pty's macOS spawn-helper. The Go PTY code has no helper file and Go modules run no install scripts, so there is nothing to exempt.
The exemption lets node-pty's install script select or compile its native addon. The Go replacement is pure Go built with CGO_ENABLED=0, so no native build step and no install script exist.

title: The terminal's foreground process group is inferred from the process table because node-pty hides the master descriptor

reason: The Go harness owns the PTY master descriptor and reads the foreground process group with one ioctl (TIOCGPGRP) on Linux and macOS, replacing a /proc read on Linux and a ps child process per query on macOS.

title: Windows terminals require node-pty's bundled OpenConsole through an experimental option, to work around a byte-level prompt comparison

reason: The Go design uses the operating system's ConPTY by default and recognises a prompt from the emulated screen, where the two byte forms that differ between console hosts give the same text. A different console host is operator configuration, not a bundled requirement. The reasoning is an inference to be confirmed on Windows Server 2022.

title: Release pipeline steps that exist only because the PTY is a native addon with helper binaries

reason: A statically linked Go binary contains the PTY code, so the manylinux rebuild and glibc symbol check, the macOS deployment-target check of spawn-helper, the -spawn-helper sidecar beside each executable, the archive unpack rules and the per-platform conpty file policy have no counterpart.

title: On Windows node-pty cannot be relied on to kill a terminal or report its exit, so cleanup uses taskkill, polls the process table and fabricates the exit result

reason: The Go harness creates the terminal's process itself and keeps its handle: exit is observed by waiting on the handle and termination is TerminateProcess or a job object, so no exit notification from a library is needed (DH-LIB-NODEPTY-R6).

title: About two dozen product packages start programs outside the subprocess service, each with its own deadline, output-limit, kill and environment handling

reason: In the Go design one harness process package is the only non-test importer of os/exec, enforced by a source check (DH-LIB-NODEPROC-R14), so lookup, Windows command lines, environment scrubbing, tree ownership and cleanup are the same for every program the harness starts.

title: Process starting, line input and interpreter processes: os/exec, os/signal, context and bufio in one harness process package, with golang.org/x/sys for tree owners
Terminals are allocated by harness code on golang.org/x/sys, with no cgo and no helper executable
Windows uses the operating system's console host; another host is configuration, never a bundled requirement
The host emulator sits behind one harness interface; go-headless-term is its first, provisional implementation
The snapshot serializer and the marks are harness code
One process package starts every program, from an argument list, with an explicit rule for Windows command lines
A process tree is owned by an operating-system object held by the harness, not by a scan or a helper process
A program started on a terminal sees a terminal of the requested size and type; input and output are ordered bytes
The child leads its session, owns the terminal, and the foreground group is read from the terminal
Resize reaches the program; resize after exit fails with a stable error
Exit is observed with code or signal, including a kill from outside the harness
Signals reach the foreground group on POSIX; Windows interrupt is Ctrl-C and unsupported signals are refused
Close leaves no descriptor, handle, goroutine or console host; allocation failure is one stable error
Closing a Windows terminal never blocks, on old and current Windows versions
Windows default needs no file beside the binary; a configured console host is used or fails loudly
The product builds with CGO_ENABLED=0 for every release target; a Windows terminal inside a job dies with the job
Readers observe only states that follow a whole prefix of the output chunks
Terminal queries produce ordered replies, none when turned off, and a bounded number under flood
History and memory stay bounded and arbitrary bytes cause no panic
A snapshot replayed into xterm.js equals an xterm.js that received the original bytes
Text reads join wrapped rows, trim padding and show the alternate screen as displayed
Marks return the lines since the mark, report truncation and handle a screen switch
Resize keeps the cursor in the grid; reads after close fail; an emulator panic does not stop the session
Two byte forms of the same prompt give the same text left of the cursor
Conformance corpus: the adapter's grid equals xterm.js's for recorded shell and full-screen sessions
Windows arguments reach an ordinary program unchanged, for a table and for generated inputs
Batch files are refused by default and unsafe arguments are refused with opt-in; no injected command runs
Lookup uses the child's PATH, refuses relative paths and never uses the current directory
The child's environment is scrubbed, extended and trimmed as requested
Cancellation escalates after the grace period; exit and tree-gone are separate waits
A grandchild that detaches itself is still terminated and still counted
Children after the harness is killed or signalled match the per-system guarantee
No suspended Windows process is left when the harness dies mid-start; background children open no window
Collection, spill, detached launch and a long-lived piped child behave as specified
Only the process package imports os/exec; confirmation refuses without a terminal
Run distinguishes not started, non-zero exit, deadline, cancellation; a deadline kills the tree at once
Captured output is byte-exact and an exceeded limit stops the run and is reported
A stream is appended to a file across runs
A tool installed as .exe or .cmd starts by bare name on Windows, through the process package
Lookup against an explicit PATH finds, skips and refuses as specified
Command lines split into literal simple commands or are reported as not analysable
Quote then parse returns the original list for generated strings
